196 FERC ¶ 61,226
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER REJECTING NOTICE OF CANCELLATION

 (Issued September 22, 2026)

On July 24, 2026, pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and part 35.15 of the Commission’s regulations, Commonwealth Edison Company (ComEd) submitted a Notice of Cancellation of the executed Transmission Security Agreement between ComEd and PowerHouse Hillwood Holding, LLC (Hillwood, and together with ComEd, the Parties) (Transmission Security Agreement).  As discussed below, we reject the Notice of Cancellation, without prejudice. 
Background and Overview of Notice of Cancellation
On January 13, 2026, ComEd filed the Transmission Security Agreement as an executed agreement by and between ComEd and Hillwood.  ComEd stated that it intended to provide retail electric delivery services to a data center that Hillwood was constructing, including by constructing, maintaining, and operating transmission facilities, pursuant to the applicable rate schedule in ComEd’s retail electric service tariff on file with the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC).  ComEd stated that the Transmission Security Agreement recognizes that, following execution and prior to the commencement of construction of or modifications to transmission facilities, other steps may need to be taken, such as preparing and filing applications for approval by the ICC.  The Commission accepted the Transmission Security Agreement on March 10, 2026, noting that the ICC retains authority to establish terms of retail service between ComEd and Hillwood.
ComEd states that it is cancelling the Transmission Security Agreement because: (1) the underlying retail service application has been cancelled; and (2) ComEd believes Hillwood is in breach of the Transmission Security Agreement for failure to provide the required credit support.  ComEd explains that the underlying retail service application has been cancelled because Hillwood has failed to comply with certain terms and conditions of ComEd’s electric retail service tariff on file with the Illinois Commerce Commission.  ComEd argues that the required credit support is an essential element of the Transmission Security Agreement framework that facilitates the overall goal of guarding against shifting costs and risks to other customers over the term of the Transmission Security Agreement, as well as minimizing the risk that the presence of oversized or unrealistic applications unreasonably harms other applicants waiting to interconnect to ComEd’s system.  ComEd states that, as disclosed by Hillwood in a  July 20, 2026 complaint filed against ComEd in Cook County, Illinois, on April 14, 2026, Hillwood provided ComEd with a letter of credit in the amount of $1.00 and claims that the $1.00 letter of credit satisfied the credit support obligations under the Transmission Security Agreement.
ComEd states that the Parties have exhausted the dispute resolution process provided in the Transmission Security Agreement, without reaching resolution on the issue of the required credit support.  ComEd states that, upon cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement, the Parties will have no remaining obligations under the Transmission Security Agreement and asserts that no parties will be affected or harmed by the cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement.  Without an active retail service application, ComEd states that it has no need to maintain the Transmission Security Agreement on file with the Commission on and after the requested effective date.  
ComEd requests that the Commission accept the Notice of Cancellation without suspension, hearing, or condition, effective July 25, 2026, the day after the filing was submitted.  ComEd requests waiver of the Commission’s 60-day period notice requirement to permit this effective date.  ComEd argues good cause exists to grant a   July 25, 2026 effective date for the cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement because the underlying retail service application has been cancelled and Hillwood has failed to provide the required credit support.  ComEd states that, to the extent any Commission regulation or other applicable requirements are not satisfied by the filing, ComEd requests waiver of those requirements as well.
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of ComEd’s filing was published in the Federal Register,                                   91 Fed. Reg. 47829 (July 29, 2026), with interventions and protests due on or before August 14, 2026.  Timely motions to intervene were filed by Hillwood and Constellation Energy Generation, LLC.  A timely protest was filed by Hillwood on August 14, 2026.  ComEd filed a motion for leave to answer and answer on August 31, 2026.  Hillwood filed an answer in opposition to ComEd’s motion for leave to answer and answer on September 11, 2026.  ComEd filed a second motion for leave to answer and answer on September 15, 2026.  Hillwood filed a second answer on September 16, 2026.  ComEd filed a third answer in response to Hillwood’s second answer on September 17, 2026. 
Hillwood’s Protest
Hillwood argues that ComEd’s notice of cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory, and the Commission should therefore reject the notice.  Hillwood argues that, in the alternative, the Commission should suspend the effective date for five-months, set the matter for hearing, and hold the hearing in abeyance to allow the Parties to participate in settlement before a Commission settlement judge.  
Hillwood argues that the dispute between ComEd and Hillwood centers on when the Year 1 credit support under the Transmission Security Agreement is due.  Hillwood argues that ComEd filed a contract that imposes significant credit support obligations starting with Year 1 but has now demanded that level of security prior to Year 1.  Hillwood argues that when Hillwood indicated that it would abide by the filed terms, ComEd sought to cancel the Transmission Security Agreement while leveraging pretextual retail-service and land-transfer demands to coerce a posting that the Transmission Security Agreement does not require.  
Hillwood claims that, once Dispute Resolution procedures ran their course and failed to reach a resolution, Hillwood filed a lawsuit against ComEd in state court.  Hillwood states that ComEd filed to remove the proceeding to federal court, and a federal court decision on whether to remand is pending in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.  Hillwood further states that, following the filing of the lawsuit, ComEd initiated the instant proceeding to cancel the Transmission Security Agreement and disclosed that ComEd had cancelled the retail service application.  
Hillwood states that it posted a $1 letter of credit in satisfaction of the obligation to post a letter of credit within 30 days of the effective date in absence of an amount specified in the Transmission Security Agreement for pre-Year 1 credit support.  Hillwood claims that there is neither any provision in the Transmission Security Agreement providing that additional credit support must be posted in 2026, nor any stated rationale for credit support of such magnitude.  
Hillwood argues that the Commission has previously rejected or dismissed similar proposed cancellations where there was a question as to whether the contract to be canceled permitted the proposed cancellation.
ComEd’s First Answer
ComEd argues that when a customer breaches its retail obligations and “flouts a Commission-accepted federal rate,” it is just, reasonable, nondiscriminatory, and in the public interest to cancel the Transmission Security Agreement.  ComEd disputes Hillwood’s argument that the cancellation is “extra-contractual,” stating that section 14 of the Transmission Security Agreement does not list breach among its enumerated termination grounds.  ComEd claims that nothing in the Transmission Security Agreement deprives ComEd of the right to cancel the Transmission Security Agreement and that nothing indicates the stated termination triggers are exclusive.  ComEd argues that Hillwood’s interpretation of the Transmission Security Agreement eliminates core consumer protections.  ComEd reasserts that its proposed cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement identifies two independent grounds for cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement:  (1) the underlying service application (Retail Application) has been cancelled; and (2) Hillwood is in breach of the Transmission Security Agreement for its failure to provide the required credit support.   
ComEd argues that Hillwood failed to meet its electric retail service tariff requirements, thus warranting cancellation of the underlying retail application.  ComEd argues that, because it terminated the retail application pursuant to the its retail service tariff, cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement is just and reasonable as well.  Further, ComEd argues that everything in the Transmission Security Agreement is premised on the assumption that there is a project taking retail service, and absent such a project, the Transmission Security Agreement serves no purpose.  ComEd states Hillwood has not raised the issue of Hillwood’s retail application cancellation with the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) – the tribunal that maintains jurisdiction to decide such issues.  Further, ComEd states that Hillwood has withdrawn its request for a federal court to issue a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction related to the retail application.  Under this argument, ComEd asserts that maintaining the Transmission Security Agreement on file would serve no purpose.   
ComEd explains that the credit support is an essential element of the Transmission Security Agreement framework.  ComEd argues that:  (1) nothing in the Transmission Security Agreement authorizes a $1.00 Credit Support Requirement; (2) a $1.00 letter of credit is indistinguishable from no letter at all; and (3) accepting Hillwood’s interpretation would render the Transmission Security Agreement’s credit support requirements meaningless.  ComEd argues that the only way to protect customers is if the developer provides the full letter of credit at the outset, which, ComEd argues, is what the Transmission Security Agreement is designed to do and requires.  
ComEd argues the Commission has found it just and reasonable to authorize the cancellation of a Commission-jurisdictional contract where:  (1) the agreement no longer serves a purpose; (2) the counterparty fails to cure a breach of its contractual obligations during the interconnection process; (3) continuing to enforce the contract following breach harms other market participants and the public interest; and (4) the developer was unable to secure necessary certificates to construct the facilities.  Additionally, ComEd states that the Commission has previously accepted the cancellation of interconnection service agreements over a developer’s objection.
ComEd challenges Hillwood’s reliance on Commission precedent rejecting other cancellation filings where the Commission applied Arkla.   ComEd argues that Arkla issues are irrelevant in the context of an FPA section 205 filing.  ComEd further argues that the Arkla factors nevertheless support Commission consideration of the dispute.  ComEd argues that the first factor is met because this dispute requires the interpretation of a Commission accepted rate schedule in light of representations made to the Commission during the approval process and the Commission’s own reasoning in accepting it.  ComEd argues the second factor is met because the Commission accepted the Transmission Security Agreement in reliance on its safeguards to customers and the question of who bears the risk of a failed data center project is a question central to the Commission’s regulatory agenda.  Lastly, ComEd argues there is a need for uniformity of interpretation because the Transmission Security Agreement follows a standardized form filed for other projects and leaving its construction to scattered forms could result in inconsistent interpretations.
Hillwood’s First Answer
Hillwood argues that the Commission should:  (1) reject ComEd’s answer as untimely filed without the requisite support for late filing and as an impermissible pleading for which leave to file is unwarranted; (2) apply Arkla and decline to exercise primary jurisdiction over the underlying contract dispute; and (3) reject ComEd’s notice of cancellation without prejudice pending resolution by the court of the underlying contract dispute.  Hillwood argues that the Commission should deny ComEd’s answer because Rule 213(a)(2) bars an answer to a protest unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  Hillwood states that the Commission has repeatedly rejected answers to protests pursuant to this rule.  
Hillwood also argues that under Arkla the Commission should decline to exercise primary jurisdiction over the parties’ “simple contract dispute,” reject the Notice of Cancellation, and permit the Illinois courts to resolve that dispute under Illinois law.  As to the first Arkla factor, Hillwood argues that resolution of the issues turns on standard contract principles, does not address matters arising under the FPA, and therefore, does not involve matters within the Commission’s particular area of expertise.  Hillwood highlights ComEd’s own statements that Illinois law governs the breach of contract dispute.  As to the second Arkla factor, Hillwood asserts that there is no need for uniformity in resolving the parties’ dispute, which, according to Hillwood, relates exclusively to the parties’ rights and obligations under the Transmission Security Agreement.  Hillwood highlights ComEd’s statements in support of application of the Transmission Security Agreement’s Mobile-Sierra provision, asserting that the Transmission Security Agreement is a bilateral agreement between two parties, not reflecting a rate of general applicability.  Hillwood also asserts that lack of uniform interpretation is not a concern, because Illinois law governs the dispute.  As to the third Arkla factor, Hillwood emphasizes that the relevant query is limited to whether this dispute is important to the Commission’s regulatory responsibilities.  
Hillwood argues that, if the Commission exercises primary jurisdiction, then under a proper interpretation of the Transmission Security Agreement, the Notice of Cancellation should be rejected.  Hillwood states that none of ComEd’s arguments regarding the Year 1 Credit Support would support ComEd’s requested credit support amount.  Hillwood argues that instead of showing that the Notice of Cancellation is just and reasonable under FPA section 205, ComEd asserts that continuation of the Transmission Security Agreement under Hillwood’s interpretation would harm the public interest under Mobile-Sierra.  Hillwood asserts that ComEd muddles the Mobile-Sierra analysis to support cancellation and, moreover, assumes that under Mobile-Sierra cancellation is the appropriate resolution of the parties’ dispute.  Hillwood states the parties agree that Illinois law governs the entire dispute, and, says Hillwood, Illinois courts are best situated to resolve it and provide any remedy.
ComEd’s Second Answer
ComEd states that Hillwood is no longer seeking injunctive relief in federal district court and is now only pursuing damages.  ComEd argues that because Hillwood withdrew its request for injunctive relief regarding the retail application, and because there is no active retail application, there is no project taking retail service for the Transmission Security Agreement to support.
ComEd opposes Hillwood’s argument that the Commission should not exercise primary jurisdiction under Arkla.  ComEd states that the federal district court already deferred to the Commission on these issues.  ComEd further asserts that Hillwood erroneously frames the issue here as whether the Commission should adjudicate a private contract dispute, but the issue is whether to accept a notice of cancellation filed under FPA section 205, which only the Commission can decide.  ComEd states that if the Commission does not accept the cancellation based on ComEd’s termination of the retail application, then whether Hillwood’s $1 letter of credit breached the Transmission Security Agreement is not a collateral matter the Commission may leave to others; it is the predicate for the FPA section 205 determination before it.  ComEd asserts the Commission cannot decline jurisdiction over that question without declining to perform its own statutory function.  ComEd argues that in any case the Arkla factors are easily met for the reasons set forth in its First Answer and that this case is similar to other Commission decisions exercising jurisdiction over contract disputes.
Hillwood’s Second Answer
Hillwood argues that ComEd has misrepresented the posture of the federal district court case and that Hillwood is still pursuing injunctive relief.  Hillwood additionally argues that, regarding the credit support requirement, ComEd misquoted the Transmission Security Agreement to the Commission by selectively and inaccurately quoting from the Transmission Security Agreement.  Hillwood argues that ComEd incorrectly claims that Hillwood is advancing a “new Arkla argument,” because ComEd has already responded to the authorities Hillwood cites to in its initial protest.  Hillwood argues that ComEd’s second answer publicly discloses information ComEd has previously designated as privileged and confidential.  
ComEd’s Third Answer 
ComEd disputes Hillwood’s statement that ComEd’s second answer publicly discloses information ComEd previously designated as privileged and confidential.  ComEd states that it does not consider the general magnitude of the early termination fee in the Transmission Security Agreement to be privileged information and that the parties have disclosed similar information publicly to the court without requesting redaction.
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 
18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the timely, unopposed motions to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding. 
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 
18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept ComEd’s and Hillwood’s answers because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
In evaluating ComEd’s proposed Notice of Cancellation, it is relevant whether ComEd has the right to unilaterally terminate the Transmission Security Agreement in these circumstances.  We note that the Parties disagree as to how key terms of the Transmission Security Agreement should be interpreted, and that the Parties currently are involved in litigation in federal district court in Illinois regarding that disagreement, including with respect to the Transmission Security Agreement’s letter of credit requirements.  
In a dispute over the interpretation of a jurisdictional contract, the Commission decides whether to assert primary jurisdiction over the contract dispute based on the three-part test established in Arkla v. Hall: 
Whether the Commission should assert jurisdiction over contractual issues otherwise litigable in state courts depends, we think, on three factors. Those factors are:  (1) whether the Commission possesses some special expertise which makes the case peculiarly appropriate for Commission decision;     (2) whether there is a need for uniformity of interpretation of the type of question raised by the dispute; and (3) whether the case is important in relation to the regulatory responsibilities of the Commission.
In applying the Arkla factors to this case, we decline to exercise primary jurisdiction.  First, we find that the Commission does not possess some special expertise in interpreting the Transmission Security Agreement in this particular case, including its letter of credit provisions.  To the extent that those provisions are ambiguous, a court is at least as well positioned as the Commission to gather extrinsic evidence as to the Parties’ respective intent in negotiating those provisions.  Second, we find that there does not appear to be a need for uniformity of contract interpretation of the type of question raised by this dispute, as the dispute involves the interpretation of the terms of a bilateral agreement between only these parties and whether termination is permitted under the particular facts here.  Third, to the extent that the Parties’ dispute is important to the regulatory responsibilities of the Commission, we find that consideration does not sufficiently outweigh the other Arkla factors to warrant the Commission’s assertion of primary jurisdiction.  
Consistent with prior cases involving proposed cancellations under FPA       section 205 where the Commission declined to exercise primary jurisdiction, we reject without prejudice ComEd’s proposed cancellation of the Transmission Security Agreement.     
The Commission orders:

The proposed Notice of Cancellation is hereby rejected, as discussed in the body of the order.

By the Commission.  Chairman Swett and Commissioner See are concurring with a

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


(Issued September 22, 2026)

SWETT, Chairman, and SEE, Commissioner, concurring:

In today’s order we decline to wade into the ongoing evidentiary morass of a commercial contract dispute best left in the perfectly competent venue of the Northern District of Illinois.  Though we decline to assert primary jurisdiction over the interpretation of ambiguous contract terms involving credit support, our commitment to fair cost allocation, ratepayer protection, and regulatory clarity remains unwavering. 
The Commission is taking intrepid action to ensure that transmission costs triggered by large loads are allocated fairly, transparently, and consistently.  Today’s order only reaffirms the criticality of the potential reforms that we proposed in the show cause proceedings underway across the country.  It is more important than ever that we develop clear and consistent terms to integrate large loads with the transmission system.  It is also more important than ever that RTO/ISOs and their transmission owners may propose pro forma Cost Recovery Agreements.  And finally, it is more important than ever that any such agreements contain strong, consistent language that both protects customers from improper cost shifting and provides certainty to contracting parties.  Establishing such pathways will leave less room for contracting error or ambiguity that requires adjudication, such as the subject of today’s order.
We remain committed to leading this Commission’s prompt review of any RTO/ISO and transmission provider proposals to resolve the issues raised in our show cause proceedings and, with input from stakeholders, moving swiftly to establish necessary reforms.  The future is bright.  
For these reasons, we respectfully concur. 
____________________
Laura V. Swett
Chairman


____________________
Lindsay S. See
Commissioner
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



(Issued September 22, 2026)


ROSNER, Commissioner, concurring: 

1.	I concur in today’s order rejecting ComEd’s Notice of Cancellation.  My colleagues would allow the pending federal district court case between ComEd and PowerHouse Hillwood to proceed rather than weigh in now.  I agree and write separately to emphasize what is at stake.
2.	There is broad bipartisan consensus around the imperative to shield consumers from the costs of data centers.  The Credit Support structure at issue is supposed to serve as a security deposit that ensures the utility’s other customers, including residential customers, are not left with the bill for infrastructure if a data center does not come online as planned.
3.	A $1 letter of credit protects no one.  
One dollar cannot guarantee payment, performance, or cover infrastructure costs if a large load project does not move forward.  Those costs would then fall on households and small businesses.
As the record shows, this token amount would leave ComEd’s customers unsecured for years while grid investments are planned and built.  That outcome is precisely what the Commission sought to prevent in its order accepting the contract, saying then that “the Transmission Security Agreement includes ‘safeguards to protect customers’ that otherwise would not exist.”  The agreement’s Credit Support provisions unmistakably exist to “guarantee[] the payment and performance obligations of Hillwood.” 
This dispute also illustrates why the Commission directed the inclusion of pro forma cost‑recovery agreements in the June 2026 Large Load show cause proceedings: requiring security deposits helps ensure both project viability and transparency.  Cost-recovery agreements matter because they enable efficient and accurate planning, and ensure that project risks stay where they belong: with the developer, not the public.
Accordingly, while I join my colleagues because federal court proceedings have already been initiated, I underscore that contracts like this are where affordability questions become real for American families and small businesses.
For these reasons, I respectfully concur.
________________________
David Rosner
Commissioner
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



(Issued September 22, 2026)

LACERTE, Commissioner, concurring: 

I concur today because as this order recognizes, an action originally filed in state court and, which, as the result of removal, is now pending in federal district court, already exists.  Nonetheless, I feel compelled to comment on possible cost shifting to consumers.
Generally, a letter of credit provides a guarantee or security for a party’s obligations under an agreement and the Commission understood that to be the parties’ representation of how this Letter of Credit works when it originally accepted the Transmission Security Agreement.  For example, this Letter of Credit provides security to an early termination fee described as “tens of millions of dollars for the first 180 days, escalating thereafter to hundreds of millions of dollars.”    
The idea that $1 may provide appropriate security to any such agreement strikes me as an embarrassing legal fiction:  insulting to the underlying ratepayers, stakeholders, and the grid itself that bear the real risk of this project.  Treating that risk as collateralizable for less than the price of a cup of coffee to me trivializes the very obligations that such a guarantee purports to secure. 
If the parties valorize a deal at a dollar, regulators should be entitled to ask whether the underlying commitment by the parties to a transaction is worth any more than that.  In my view, infrastructure of this consequence deserves security that reflects its actual stakes – not a token gesture that suggests ratepayers are an afterthought.

For these reasons, I respectfully concur.


______________________________
David LaCerte
Commissioner
